Lessons.Title: Prime and Composite Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Grade 4 U01 L03, IM 2021: identify prime and composite numbers by whole-number rectangular areas and factor-pair counts. One is neither. The first-party Edulytics lesson builds on the verified 2021 teacher preparation, teacher lesson and 4-page original student PDF.
Warm-up 10 min — Choral Count: count by 2 from 0 to 30 and by 5 from 0 to 75, note common multiples 10,20,30 and continue the pattern with a partner.

Activity 1 15 min — Card Sort: Area. Source Blackline PDF was inspected visually. Original eight rectangles are A 3×8, B 3×12, C 1×18, D 3×6, E 4×6, F 6×6, G 1×7, H 4×9. Record area groups: 7 (G), 18 (C,D), 24 (A,E), 36 (B,F,H). Use grid paper or unit tiles to investigate whether another DISTINCT side pair can be made within every area group; none exists for 7. Teacher reviews group sorting and original mathematics. This text and numerical table are Edulytics-authored, not publisher artwork.

Activity 2 20 min — Prime or Composite? Complete the 2021 student task's exact area list 2,10,48,11,21,23,60,32,42,31,56. For every value find each unique whole-number factor pair, count rectangles and decide prime/composite with an explanation. The table visual is a teacher checking reference, not a prefilled student task. Rotated rectangles count once.

Lesson synthesis 10 min — Prime n>1 has one unordered factor pair; composite n>1 has more than one. Number 1 is neither prime nor composite despite area1 having a 1×1 model. Teacher asks learners to explain proofs and reflect on mathematical-community participation.

Edulytics original five-minute Cool-down, NOT publisher-source-identical: a rectangle of area 29 has only the pair (1,29), so 29 is prime. Ask student to justify, and separately explain why 1 is neither. Teacher marks drawings and explanations. Source protected publisher Cool-down was not inspected; digital exact practice handles prime/composite counts only.

KeyConcepts.Title: Factor pairs
KeyConcepts.Definition: Unordered positive whole-number pairs a,b with a×b=n.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count each rotation once; test divisors ≤√n.

KeyConcepts.Title: Prime
KeyConcepts.Definition: A positive integer greater than one with exactly one unordered factor pair.

KeyConcepts.Title: Composite
KeyConcepts.Definition: An integer greater than one with multiple unordered factor pairs.
KeyConcepts.Rule: At least one factor other than 1 and n.

KeyConcepts.Title: Neither
KeyConcepts.Definition: One is not prime and not composite.
KeyConcepts.Example: 1×1 exists but 1 is neither prime nor composite.

WorkedExamples.Title: Area 7 card
WorkedExamples.Question: Can another area-7 rectangle have a different unordered side pair?

WorkedExamples.Title: Area 48
WorkedExamples.Question: How many distinct rectangles with area 48 exist?

WorkedExamples.Title: One is neither
WorkedExamples.Question: Classify 1 as prime/composite.
Steps: A prime must have two distinct positive factors.
